If you’re creating a portfolio for a UX student or designer aiming for an entry-level position, your clients want to see evidence that you’ve thought through the design decisions and know how to apply them in practice. That doesn’t just mean drawing pretty pictures. If all the UX you’ve been doing so far has been to help the designer make design choices without understanding why those choices matter, your CV won’t have a very compelling story to tell.

If you’re preparing to present your work to clients or another audience at work, a well-crafted portfolio can help build understanding and improve communication. With an example or two, you can demonstrate to others how well you understand the design process and the implications of your work. As a side benefit, when colleagues and coworkers see the work you’ve done they’ll be amazed instead of confused and might build more confidence in your capabilities.

Research is essential in the UX practice. UX designers who can explain their thinking will have an advantage over their peers. In order to communicate your ideas well, you should have a solid understanding of other users and designers.

Here are some tips for researching and thinking through UX work:

Focus on your goals and understand how your work fits into the bigger picture. Are you trying to create an interface, improve usability or improve conversions? If you want your web app to save time, what tasks (other than “go” button) in your app’s user flow would encourage a user to take more time and effort to complete those tasks themselves instead of just clicking a button and then immediately going back to your home screen to do it again later? How will the process evolve over time to improve the UX and usability? What are the tradeoffs to consider as your goals change?
Learn about other people’s research and practice:
Talk to other designers in your organization about their UX processes. If you’re working on a large project, ask the client how they’re considering the UX.
Read blogs and articles about UX and related topics
Watch videos about UX and related topics.
Watch interviews with designers and UX practitioners.

One common problem with UX work involves the lack of communication between the product manager and the designer or the lack of understanding of the goals by both parties. Sometimes products are in the design phase before a project manager can clearly articulate what the target audience will value the most and these disagreements affect the design. Sometimes it’s simply that the developer hasn’t built the product yet, so designers aren’t able to use it to define their designs.

Understanding the goals of your clients and how your work will help achieve them will help guide your research and thinking. Once you understand what you’re trying to accomplish you can start thinking through user research techniques that will help you answer questions like how to get your ideas to the right people, how to ask effective questions to discover what your users really need and how to make sure your research doesn’t just tell you something about users that you already knew already.

You can communicate your understanding of your goals and how your work contributes to those goals by:

Using examples from your own work to help illustrate your points.
Describing your thinking around your design and research decisions. This will help communicate how you came to the decisions you made and who made those decisions.
Giving presentations to other people about your work.
Being confident and comfortable when sharing your research findings and thinking with others.
Being transparent with your clients about what has and hasn’t been done yet.
Writing down your research ideas before you start doing anything.

One useful tool for organizing your research is mind mapping. As you read, watch, and listen, take notes and start making connections and ideas in your mind. Once you have an idea for a topic you want to explore in more detail, make a simple drawing for that topic and ideas you want to include. Some common tools for creating mind maps include MindMeister, Coggle and XMind.
There are plenty of videos available on YouTube that will give you an idea of how great designers think, especially those that have been professionally produced or have been thoroughly researched by UX practitioners.
You can also use more visual tools like diagrams and cards in collaboration with other designers and stakeholders to define tasks and processes in advance.

The most important part of UX research is understanding the people you’re trying to influence. UX research isn’t just about user testing or usability testing or prototyping, it’s about studying your target audience and knowing how they think. If you don’t, you might end up with designs that completely fail to meet their needs or expectations.
